# Perles configuration

 [Add links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q7169136#sitelinks-wikipedia)                         [![This is a good article\. Click here for more information\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles*)   From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Irrational system of points and lines

 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Perles_configuration.svg/250px-Perles_configuration.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Perles_configuration.svg)The Perles configuration

In geometry, the **Perles configuration** is a system of nine points and nine lines in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) for which every combinatorially equivalent realization has at least one [irrational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_number) as one of its coordinates. It can be constructed from some of the diagonals and symmetry lines of a [regular pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_pentagon), and their crossing points. All of the realizations of the Perles configuration in the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) are equivalent to each other under [projective transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_transformation).

The Perles configuration is the smallest configuration of points and lines that cannot be realized with rational coordinates. It is named after [Micha Perles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha_Perles), who used it to construct an eight-dimensional [convex polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope) that cannot be given rational number coordinates and that has the fewest vertices (twelve) of any known irrational polytope. The Perles configuration has additional applications as a [counterexample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterexample) in the theory of [visibility graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visibility_graph) and in [graph drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_drawing).

## Construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=1)]

One way of constructing the Perles configuration is to start with a regular [pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon) and its five diagonals. These diagonals form the sides of a smaller inner pentagon nested inside the outer pentagon. Each vertex of the outer pentagon is situated opposite from a vertex of the inner pentagon. The nine points of the configuration consist of four out of the five vertices of each pentagon and the shared center of the two pentagons. Two opposite vertices are omitted, one from each pentagon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

The nine lines of the configuration consist of the five lines that are diagonals of the outer pentagon and sides of the inner pentagon, and the four lines that pass through the center and through opposite pairs of vertices from the two pentagons.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

## Projective invariance and irrationality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=2)]

A realization of the Perles configuration is defined to consist of any nine points and nine lines with the same intersection pattern. That means that a point and line intersect each other in the realization, if and only if they intersect in the configuration constructed from the regular pentagon. Every realization of this configuration in the Euclidean plane or, more generally, in the real [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) is equivalent, under a [projective transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_transformation), to a realization constructed from a regular pentagon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2) One proof of this fact assigns arbitrary [projective coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_coordinates) to the two outer points on the four-point line, the center point of the configuration, and one of the remaining two outer points. These points determine the position of one middle point on the four-point line. One then defines a parameter specifying, in terms of these coordinates, the position of the fourth point on this line. This parameter can be calculated in terms of the projective coordinates of the remaining points. The requirement that these points be collinear translates into a constraint on the parameter: it must obey the [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation) satisfied by the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio). The two solutions to this equation both produce configurations of the same type, with rearranged points. Therefore, when this parameterization is applied both to the regular pentagon realization and any other realization, the two realizations end up with the same projective coordinates, meaning that they are projectively equivalent.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

The [cross-ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-ratio) is a number defined from any four collinear points. In the realization derived from the regular pentagon, the four collinear points have cross-ratio     1 + φ   {\displaystyle 1+\varphi }  , where     φ   {\displaystyle \varphi }   is the golden ratio, an irrational number. The cross-ratio does not change under projective transformations, so it remains irrational for every realization. However, every four collinear points with rational coordinates have a rational cross ratio, so the Perles configuration cannot be realized by rational points.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2)

Answering a question of [Branko Grünbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branko_Gr%C3%BCnbaum),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2) [József Solymosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zsef_Solymosi) has proved that the Perles configuration is the smallest possible irrational configuration of points and lines: every configuration of eight or fewer points in the Euclidean plane, and lines through subsets of these points, has a combinatorially equivalent configuration with points that have rational numbers as their coordinates.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025-3)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=3)]

### In polyhedral combinatorics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=4)]

Perles used his configuration to construct the *Perles polytope*,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGouveiaMacchiaThomasWiebe2020-4) an eight-dimensional [convex polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope) with twelve vertices that can similarly be realized with real coordinates but not with rational coordinates. The points of the configuration, three of them repeated and with positive, negative, or zero signs assigned to each point, form the [affine Gale diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale_diagram) of this polytope, from which the polytope itself can be recovered.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum200394%E2%80%9395-5)

[Steinitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinitz's_theorem), characterizing the graphs of three-dimensional convex polytopes, can be strengthened to show that every three-dimensional convex polytope can be realized with rational coordinates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003244-6) However, there exist irrational polytopes in four dimensions. Therefore, the Perles polytope does not have the smallest possible dimension among irrational polytopes. However, the Perles polytope has the fewest vertices of any known irrational polytope.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum200396a-7)

### In discrete geometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=5)]

The existence of irrational configurations such as the Perles configuration forms a counterexample to a 2021 conjecture of Mozhgan Mirzaei and Andrew Suk, on the maximum number of point-line incidences among     n   {\displaystyle n}   points and     n   {\displaystyle n}   lines. Without restriction, this maximum number is proportional to      n  4  /  3     {\displaystyle n^{4/3}}  . Mirzaei and Suk conjectured that forbidding any smaller point–line configuration from appearing would lead to an asymptotic reduction in the number of incidences. However, their conjecture is false for irrational forbidden configurations, such as the Perles configuration. There exist systems of     n   {\displaystyle n}   points arranged in an integer grid and     n   {\displaystyle n}   lines through these points that have a number of incidences proportional to      n  4  /  3     {\displaystyle n^{4/3}}  . Because their points lie on a grid, these systems avoid the Perles configuration and any irrational configuration, in contradiction to the conjecture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025-3)

As part of a proof that recognizing the [visibility graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visibility_graph) of finite point sets is hard for the [existential theory of the reals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_theory_of_the_reals), Cardinal and Hoffman in 2017 showed how to convert problems of testing whether [pseudoline arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_of_pseudolines) can be straightened into equivalent problems of visibility graph recognition. The same conversion, applied to the Perles configuration, produces finite point sets for which any other point set with the same visibility graph must include an irrational coordinate. Because of these irrational visibility graphs, it is not possible to test whether a graph is a visibility graph merely by checking all point configurations in a large enough integer grid.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTECardinalHoffmann2017-8)

### Other

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=6)]

A [matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid) can be defined from the Perles configuration, called the *Perles matroid*.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorey2021Figure_2_(Figure_8.1_of_arXiv_version)-9) It has the points of the configuration as its elements; a subset of at most three elements is independent when it does not consist of three points on one of the lines of the configuration. This matroid and its [dual matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_matroid) have been applied in characterizing certain classes of matroids that are [linear matroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_matroid) over the [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)       F   4     {\displaystyle \mathbb {F} _{4}}   and over all sufficiently large fields. The Perles matroid does not have this property: it is linear over       F   4     {\displaystyle \mathbb {F} _{4}}   but not over the [rational numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number). Its nonlinearity over the rationals is inherited by any other matroid within which the Perles matroid appears as a [matroid minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid_minor).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-10) In [tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry), this matroid has been used to separate variant analogues of [matrix rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_rank) from each other.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShitov2023-11)

In [graph drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_drawing), the Perles configuration has been used to show that drawing a [planar graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_graph) with the minimum *line cover number*, the number of lines needed to cover all the edges of the drawing, may require irrational coordinates. In particular, one such graph may be formed by the diagonals and symmetry lines of the regular pentagon, without removing one of these lines to form the Perles configuration. The vertices of this graph are 16 crossing points of these lines (including the nine points of the Perles configuration); its edges connect pairs of consecutive points along each line. Covering the edges of this graph with only ten lines forces the drawing to contain a copy of the Perles configuration and therefore to have an irrational vertex.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChaplickFleszarLippRavsky2023472%E2%80%93477Section_4-12)

In [coding theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coding_theory), the Perles configuration appears in an enumeration of 9-point configurations used to count [maximum distance separable codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_distance_separable_code) over finite fields.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-13)

## History and related work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=7)]

The Perles configuration was introduced by [Micha Perles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha_Perles) in the 1960s.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-14) It is not the first known example of an irrational configuration of points and lines. In 1936, [Mac Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saunders_Mac_Lane) described an 11-point example, obtained by applying [Von Staudt's algebra of throws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Georg_Christian_von_Staudt#Algebra_of_throws) to construct a configuration corresponding to the [square root of two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root_of_two).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-15)

Regular [projective configurations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_configuration) have long been studied. These are finite systems of points and lines in which each point touches equally many lines and each line touches equally many points. However, despite being named similarly to these configurations, the Perles configuration is not regular: most of its points touch three lines and most of its lines touch three points, but there is one line of four points and one point on four lines. In this respect it differs from the [Pappus configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus_configuration), which also has nine points and nine lines, but with three points on every line and three lines through every point.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerger2010-16) Not every abstractly-described system of points and lines has a planar realization: the [Möbius–Kantor configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius%E2%80%93Kantor_configuration) of eight points and eight lines does not.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025915-17) Every regular configuration with three lines per point, three points per line, and at most 13 points, if realizable in the Euclidean plane at all, can be realized with rational coordinates. Grünbaum has conjectured that this is true for all numbers of points, but this remains an open problem.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025913-18)

Introduction

# Introduction

Perles configuration

# Perles configuration

[Add links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q7169136#sitelinks-wikipedia)                         [![This is a good article\. Click here for more information\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles*)   From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Irrational system of points and lines

 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Perles_configuration.svg/250px-Perles_configuration.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Perles_configuration.svg)The Perles configuration

In geometry, the **Perles configuration** is a system of nine points and nine lines in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) for which every combinatorially equivalent realization has at least one [irrational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_number) as one of its coordinates. It can be constructed from some of the diagonals and symmetry lines of a [regular pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_pentagon), and their crossing points. All of the realizations of the Perles configuration in the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) are equivalent to each other under [projective transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_transformation).

The Perles configuration is the smallest configuration of points and lines that cannot be realized with rational coordinates. It is named after [Micha Perles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha_Perles), who used it to construct an eight-dimensional [convex polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope) that cannot be given rational number coordinates and that has the fewest vertices (twelve) of any known irrational polytope. The Perles configuration has additional applications as a [counterexample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterexample) in the theory of [visibility graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visibility_graph) and in [graph drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_drawing).

Construction

# Construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=1)]

One way of constructing the Perles configuration is to start with a regular [pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon) and its five diagonals. These diagonals form the sides of a smaller inner pentagon nested inside the outer pentagon. Each vertex of the outer pentagon is situated opposite from a vertex of the inner pentagon. The nine points of the configuration consist of four out of the five vertices of each pentagon and the shared center of the two pentagons. Two opposite vertices are omitted, one from each pentagon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

The nine lines of the configuration consist of the five lines that are diagonals of the outer pentagon and sides of the inner pentagon, and the four lines that pass through the center and through opposite pairs of vertices from the two pentagons.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

Projective invariance and irrationality

# Projective invariance and irrationality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=2)]

A realization of the Perles configuration is defined to consist of any nine points and nine lines with the same intersection pattern. That means that a point and line intersect each other in the realization, if and only if they intersect in the configuration constructed from the regular pentagon. Every realization of this configuration in the Euclidean plane or, more generally, in the real [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) is equivalent, under a [projective transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_transformation), to a realization constructed from a regular pentagon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2) One proof of this fact assigns arbitrary [projective coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_coordinates) to the two outer points on the four-point line, the center point of the configuration, and one of the remaining two outer points. These points determine the position of one middle point on the four-point line. One then defines a parameter specifying, in terms of these coordinates, the position of the fourth point on this line. This parameter can be calculated in terms of the projective coordinates of the remaining points. The requirement that these points be collinear translates into a constraint on the parameter: it must obey the [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation) satisfied by the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio). The two solutions to this equation both produce configurations of the same type, with rearranged points. Therefore, when this parameterization is applied both to the regular pentagon realization and any other realization, the two realizations end up with the same projective coordinates, meaning that they are projectively equivalent.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiegler2008-1)

The [cross-ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-ratio) is a number defined from any four collinear points. In the realization derived from the regular pentagon, the four collinear points have cross-ratio     1 + φ   {\displaystyle 1+\varphi }  , where     φ   {\displaystyle \varphi }   is the golden ratio, an irrational number. The cross-ratio does not change under projective transformations, so it remains irrational for every realization. However, every four collinear points with rational coordinates have a rational cross ratio, so the Perles configuration cannot be realized by rational points.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2)

Answering a question of [Branko Grünbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branko_Gr%C3%BCnbaum),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003-2) [József Solymosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zsef_Solymosi) has proved that the Perles configuration is the smallest possible irrational configuration of points and lines: every configuration of eight or fewer points in the Euclidean plane, and lines through subsets of these points, has a combinatorially equivalent configuration with points that have rational numbers as their coordinates.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025-3)

Applications

# Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=3)]

In polyhedral combinatorics

# In polyhedral combinatorics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=4)]

Perles used his configuration to construct the *Perles polytope*,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGouveiaMacchiaThomasWiebe2020-4) an eight-dimensional [convex polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope) with twelve vertices that can similarly be realized with real coordinates but not with rational coordinates. The points of the configuration, three of them repeated and with positive, negative, or zero signs assigned to each point, form the [affine Gale diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale_diagram) of this polytope, from which the polytope itself can be recovered.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum200394%E2%80%9395-5)

[Steinitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinitz's_theorem), characterizing the graphs of three-dimensional convex polytopes, can be strengthened to show that every three-dimensional convex polytope can be realized with rational coordinates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum2003244-6) However, there exist irrational polytopes in four dimensions. Therefore, the Perles polytope does not have the smallest possible dimension among irrational polytopes. However, the Perles polytope has the fewest vertices of any known irrational polytope.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%BCnbaum200396a-7)

In discrete geometry

# In discrete geometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=5)]

The existence of irrational configurations such as the Perles configuration forms a counterexample to a 2021 conjecture of Mozhgan Mirzaei and Andrew Suk, on the maximum number of point-line incidences among     n   {\displaystyle n}   points and     n   {\displaystyle n}   lines. Without restriction, this maximum number is proportional to      n  4  /  3     {\displaystyle n^{4/3}}  . Mirzaei and Suk conjectured that forbidding any smaller point–line configuration from appearing would lead to an asymptotic reduction in the number of incidences. However, their conjecture is false for irrational forbidden configurations, such as the Perles configuration. There exist systems of     n   {\displaystyle n}   points arranged in an integer grid and     n   {\displaystyle n}   lines through these points that have a number of incidences proportional to      n  4  /  3     {\displaystyle n^{4/3}}  . Because their points lie on a grid, these systems avoid the Perles configuration and any irrational configuration, in contradiction to the conjecture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025-3)

As part of a proof that recognizing the [visibility graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visibility_graph) of finite point sets is hard for the [existential theory of the reals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_theory_of_the_reals), Cardinal and Hoffman in 2017 showed how to convert problems of testing whether [pseudoline arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_of_pseudolines) can be straightened into equivalent problems of visibility graph recognition. The same conversion, applied to the Perles configuration, produces finite point sets for which any other point set with the same visibility graph must include an irrational coordinate. Because of these irrational visibility graphs, it is not possible to test whether a graph is a visibility graph merely by checking all point configurations in a large enough integer grid.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTECardinalHoffmann2017-8)

Other

# Other

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=6)]

A [matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid) can be defined from the Perles configuration, called the *Perles matroid*.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorey2021Figure_2_(Figure_8.1_of_arXiv_version)-9) It has the points of the configuration as its elements; a subset of at most three elements is independent when it does not consist of three points on one of the lines of the configuration. This matroid and its [dual matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_matroid) have been applied in characterizing certain classes of matroids that are [linear matroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_matroid) over the [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)       F   4     {\displaystyle \mathbb {F} _{4}}   and over all sufficiently large fields. The Perles matroid does not have this property: it is linear over       F   4     {\displaystyle \mathbb {F} _{4}}   but not over the [rational numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number). Its nonlinearity over the rationals is inherited by any other matroid within which the Perles matroid appears as a [matroid minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid_minor).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-10) In [tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry), this matroid has been used to separate variant analogues of [matrix rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_rank) from each other.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShitov2023-11)

In [graph drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_drawing), the Perles configuration has been used to show that drawing a [planar graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_graph) with the minimum *line cover number*, the number of lines needed to cover all the edges of the drawing, may require irrational coordinates. In particular, one such graph may be formed by the diagonals and symmetry lines of the regular pentagon, without removing one of these lines to form the Perles configuration. The vertices of this graph are 16 crossing points of these lines (including the nine points of the Perles configuration); its edges connect pairs of consecutive points along each line. Covering the edges of this graph with only ten lines forces the drawing to contain a copy of the Perles configuration and therefore to have an irrational vertex.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChaplickFleszarLippRavsky2023472%E2%80%93477Section_4-12)

In [coding theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coding_theory), the Perles configuration appears in an enumeration of 9-point configurations used to count [maximum distance separable codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_distance_separable_code) over finite fields.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-13)

History and related work

# History and related work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Perles_configuration&action=edit&section=7)]

The Perles configuration was introduced by [Micha Perles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha_Perles) in the 1960s.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-14) It is not the first known example of an irrational configuration of points and lines. In 1936, [Mac Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saunders_Mac_Lane) described an 11-point example, obtained by applying [Von Staudt's algebra of throws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Georg_Christian_von_Staudt#Algebra_of_throws) to construct a configuration corresponding to the [square root of two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root_of_two).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-15)

Regular [projective configurations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_configuration) have long been studied. These are finite systems of points and lines in which each point touches equally many lines and each line touches equally many points. However, despite being named similarly to these configurations, the Perles configuration is not regular: most of its points touch three lines and most of its lines touch three points, but there is one line of four points and one point on four lines. In this respect it differs from the [Pappus configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus_configuration), which also has nine points and nine lines, but with three points on every line and three lines through every point.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerger2010-16) Not every abstractly-described system of points and lines has a planar realization: the [Möbius–Kantor configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius%E2%80%93Kantor_configuration) of eight points and eight lines does not.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025915-17) Every regular configuration with three lines per point, three points per line, and at most 13 points, if realizable in the Euclidean plane at all, can be realized with rational coordinates. Grünbaum has conjectured that this is true for all numbers of points, but this remains an open problem.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perles_configuration#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolymosi2025913-18)
